analysis.investment_thesis: INOX India is a genuinely high-quality niche industrial business — fortress balance sheet (D/E 0.10), exceptional ROCE of 38%, and steady 12% revenue CAGR — but priced at 53.5x P/E and near-zero FCF yield, it demands perfection that industrial capital equipment businesses rarely deliver. At these valuations, I would need to overpay by 2.5–3x what I consider fair for even an outstanding business.
key_strengths: Fortress balance sheet — D/E of 0.10, borrowings reduced from 145 Cr (2020) to near-negligible levels before modest recent uptick
Outstanding capital efficiency — ROCE 38%, ROE 29%, operating margins of ~20% are exceptional for industrial machinery
Strong promoter conviction — 75% holding, stable; and niche positioning in cryogenic/LNG/hydrogen infrastructure with long-term secular demand
key_risks: Valuation is prohibitive — P/E 53.5x vs my preferred 12–20x; FCF yield essentially zero (FCF turned -3 Cr in FY25); no margin of safety whatsoever
Net profit CAGR only 2.7% over 6 years (FY19–25) despite 12.3% revenue growth — earnings quality is diluted by volatile other income (28→48→15→21→19→30→48 Cr) and prior anomalies
Capex accelerating sharply (44→47→98→125 Cr) in an order-driven B2B business — lumpy revenues and project execution risk are not the steady consumer-demand predictability I require
red_flags: FCF yield is negative in FY25 — Market cap 13,539 Cr, FCF = -3 Cr; even FY24 FCF of 32 Cr yields a negligible 0.24%, far below my 5% minimum
Sector mismatch — industrial capital equipment is project/order-cycle driven, the opposite of the predictable consumer-demand businesses I understand and trust
Net profit in FY19 was anomalously high at 193 Cr on 650 Cr revenue (29.7% net margin vs 17–19% in recent years), inflated by other income — distorts long-term PAT CAGR
analysis.detailed_analysis:
INOX India is a well-run business and I respect it. The ROCE of 38% tells me management deploys capital skillfully, debt has been almost eliminated (D/E 0.10), and the 75% promoter stake demonstrates conviction. Revenue has grown steadily at 12.3% CAGR — right in my comfort zone. The company's exposure to LNG infrastructure, green hydrogen, and aerospace/cryogenic applications gives it genuine long-term relevance. In isolation, this is the kind of quiet industrial compounder one might admire.

However, at 53.5x trailing P/E and 41x EV/EBITDA, the market has already priced in a decade of flawless execution. My preferred entry for a quality industrial business is 15–20x earnings, not 53x. Free cash flow turned negative in FY25 as capex jumped to 125 Cr — the business is in an investment cycle, which is fine, but paying 13,539 Cr market cap for a company generating -3 Cr FCF is not value investing, it is speculation on future cash flows. I built DMart by buying quality at fair prices and holding for decades; I would not pay a 3x premium simply because the business is good. I will watch this one from the sidelines and revisit if valuation corrects to 20–25x earnings.
